questions.q: A director shoots an actor's neutral face once, then cuts it after a shot of a coffin and, separately, after a shot of a birthday cake. Audiences see grief, then joy. What explains this?
choices: The actor's micro-expressions changed between takes
The Kuleshov effect: viewers read the face through the shot it's cut against
The 180-degree rule
Deep focus linking foreground and background
questions.explain: The same shot takes its meaning from its neighbours; the audience supplies the emotion.

questions.q: What's the most accurate thing to say about Kuleshov's original experiment?
choices: Its footage survives and has been confirmed by every replication
It was invented by Hitchcock in 1964
The footage is lost, accounts of it vary, and modern replications give mixed results
It was a 1990s neuroscience study
questions.explain: It's a well-observed tendency resting on a shaky founding story.

questions.q: In a dialogue scene, a character hears that her brother has died. Which shot will usually carry the most meaning?
choices: The reaction shot of the listener
A wide establishing shot of the room
A close-up of the speaker delivering the line
An insert of the clock
questions.explain: The line says what's said; the listener's face shows what it means.

questions.q: A character looks off-screen to the left, and the next shot shows a gun on a table. What links the two shots for the audience?
choices: A jump cut
A Dutch angle
A match cut on shape
An eyeline match
questions.explain: A look off-screen followed by its object builds space and connects the look to what's seen.

questions.q: A screenwriter fills stage directions with 'she looks devastated, then furious, then resigned.' What would a Kuleshov-minded director suggest instead?
choices: Add a voice-over explaining her feelings
Give the image she's reacting to, and let a simpler face take its meaning from the cut
Cross the line to disorient the audience
Shoot the whole scene in one long take
questions.explain: A face that shows too much leaves the viewer nothing to do.

questions.q: Who is wrongly but often credited with inventing the close-up?
choices: D. W. Griffith
Sergei Eisenstein
G. A. Smith
Carl Theodor Dreyer
questions.explain: Close views appear in films around 1900; Griffith's contribution was using them for emotion within a story.

questions.q: A TV news crew films the interviewer nodding sympathetically after the interview and cuts those shots in. Why can this be an ethical problem?
choices: It breaks the 180-degree rule
It's a jump cut
Reaction shots can change how an answer seems to land, implying a response that never happened
It uses the male gaze
questions.explain: The Kuleshov effect works in news as well as fiction, which is why 'noddies' are controversial.

ideas: Which approach says the same unchanged face can seem hungry, grieving or tender depending on the shot it's cut against?
Which approach says the listener's reaction often matters more than the line being spoken?
